concepts.name: First Buddhist Council: Venue, Patronage, and Purpose
key_dimensions: Held at Saptaparni Cave (Rajagriha) under Ajatashatru's patronage — UPSC trap: king was Ajatashatru, not Bimbisara
Presided over by Mahakassapa; Ananda recited Sutta Pitaka, Upali recited Vinaya Pitaka
Primary purpose: to preserve the Buddha's teachings immediately after his Mahaparinirvana (483 BCE)
Abhidhamma Pitaka NOT compiled here — common misconception to exploit

concepts.name: Second Buddhist Council: Schism and the Vaishali Controversy
key_dimensions: Held at Vaishali (~383 BCE), ~100 years after First Council; presided over by Sabakami
Core dispute: Ten Points of Laxity (Dasa Vatthuni) practiced by Vajjian monks — nature of these relaxations
Patronage under Kalasoka (Kakavarna) of Shishunaga dynasty — NOT a Mauryan king (common trap)
Result: First formal schism — Sthaviravadins vs. Mahasanghikas, marking the root of Hinayana-Mahayana divergence

concepts.name: The Ten Points of Laxity (Dasa Vatthuni) — Cause of Second Council
key_dimensions: Specific ten relaxations claimed by Vajjian monks (e.g., using salt stored in horn, eating after midday, accepting gold/silver)
Orthodox Sthaviravadins declared these violations of Vinaya; their rejection led to the split
UPSC trap: distinguish these disciplinary issues from doctrinal disputes that caused later schisms
Significance: shows that early Buddhism split over monastic discipline, not metaphysical doctrine

concepts.name: Third Buddhist Council: Pataliputra and Ashoka's Role
key_dimensions: Held at Pataliputra (~250 BCE) under Emperor Ashoka's patronage; presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa
Purpose: purge the Sangha of heretics and non-Buddhist elements who had infiltrated monastic order
Compilation of Abhidhamma Pitaka and the Kathavatthu (Moggaliputta Tissa's refutation of heretical views)
Decision to send Dhamma missions abroad — Mahinda to Sri Lanka, Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka, missions to Greece, Egypt etc.

concepts.name: Kathavatthu: Significance and Authorship
key_dimensions: Authored by Moggaliputta Tissa during/after Third Council — part of Pali Canon's Abhidhamma Pitaka
Content: refutes 219 heretical propositions; key source for understanding early Buddhist sectarian debates
UPSC trap: Kathavatthu is the only Abhidhamma text attributed to a specific historical author (not the Buddha)
Distinguishing it from Milindapanha (dialogue between Nagasena and Menander) — both are philosophical texts but different contexts

concepts.name: Fourth Buddhist Council: Two Competing Traditions
key_dimensions: Two rival 'Fourth Councils': Theravada tradition (Sri Lanka, ~1st century BCE under Vattagamani Abhaya) and Sarvastivada tradition (Kashmir, ~1st–2nd century CE under Kanishka)
UPSC critical trap: Kanishka's council is recognized in Mahayana/northern tradition; Vattagamani's is in Theravada/southern tradition
Kanishka's council: held at Kundalavana (Kashmir), presided by Vasumitra; produced Mahavibhasha commentary
Vattagamani's council: first time Pali Canon was committed to writing (palm-leaf manuscripts) at Aluvihara, Sri Lanka

concepts.name: Kanishka's Buddhist Council: Mahavibhasha and Sarvastivada
key_dimensions: Presided by Vasumitra; Ashvaghosha (author of Buddhacharita) was also associated — his role is debated
Output: Mahavibhasha Shastra — encyclopedic commentary on Abhidharma; led to the school called Vaibhashika
Represents the Sarvastivada school's consolidation — doctrine that dharmas exist in past, present, and future
Geographic significance: held in Kashmir — marks northward shift of Buddhist scholarship toward Central Asia and China

concepts.name: Sthaviravada vs. Mahasanghika: Root of the Great Schism
key_dimensions: Emerged from Second Council (~383 BCE) — Sthaviravadins (elders, orthodox) vs. Mahasanghikas (great assembly, progressive)
Doctrinal differences: nature of the Arhat, concept of the ideal monk vs. Bodhisattva ideal — seeds of Hinayana vs. Mahayana
Mahasanghika's more liberal view of the Buddha's nature laid groundwork for the transcendent Buddha concept in Mahayana
UPSC trap: Theravada (surviving today in Sri Lanka/SE Asia) descends from Sthaviravada, NOT directly from either extreme faction

concepts.name: Three Pitakas (Tripitaka): Compilation Across Councils
key_dimensions: Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules): associated with First Council (Upali); Sutta Pitaka (discourses): First Council (Ananda)
Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophical analysis): Third Council (Pataliputra) — NOT First Council, key UPSC trap
Pali Canon written down only at Vattagamani's council in Sri Lanka (~1st century BCE) — oral tradition for ~400 years
Difference between Pali Canon (Theravada) and Sanskrit Tripitaka (Sarvastivada/Mahayana) — language as sectarian marker

concepts.name: Royal Patronage Pattern Across All Four Councils
key_dimensions: First: Ajatashatru (Haryanka dynasty); Second: Kalasoka (Shishunaga dynasty); Third: Ashoka (Maurya); Fourth: Kanishka (Kushana) or Vattagamani (Lankan)
UPSC trap: no Gupta emperor associated with any council — Guptas patronized Hinduism primarily; Nalanda flourished under Guptas but no formal council
Pattern shows Buddhism's dependence on royal patronage for organizational consolidation
Contrast with Jain councils: Pataliputra council of Jains (under Chandragupta Maurya) — avoid mixing up the two

concepts.name: Moggaliputta Tissa: Role and Significance
key_dimensions: President of Third Council at Pataliputra; Ashoka's spiritual guide/mentor — shaped Ashoka's Buddhist policy
Authored Kathavatthu — only Abhidhamma text by a named historical author
Organized dispatch of nine Dhamma missions to different regions including Mahinda's mission to Sri Lanka
UPSC trap: distinguish from Nagasena (interlocutor of Milindapanha) and Ashvaghosha (Kanishka's council) — all prominent Buddhist scholars

concepts.name: Dhamma Missions Dispatched After Third Council
key_dimensions: Nine missions sent: Mahinda → Sri Lanka (Tambapanni); Sanghamitra → Sri Lanka (with Bodhi tree sapling); Dharmarakshita → Aparantaka (western India)
Missions to Yona (Greek territories), Suvarnabhumi (Burma/SE Asia), Kashmir-Gandhara — marks Buddhism's internationalization
Mahinda was Ashoka's son — UPSC trap: Sanghamitra was his daughter, sent later with a branch of the Bodhi tree
These missions are the reason Theravada Buddhism dominates Sri Lanka and SE Asia today — long-term civilizational impact

concepts.name: Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha: Kanishka's Council Associates
key_dimensions: Vasumitra: president/chair of Kanishka's council; proponent of Sarvastivada school
Ashvaghosha: poet-philosopher, author of Buddhacharita (biography of Buddha) and Saundarananda; associated with Kanishka's court
UPSC trap: Ashvaghosha predates Nagarjuna (founder of Madhyamaka) — chronological order of Buddhist philosophers matters
Mahavibhasha output of this council became foundation of Vaibhashika school — one of the four main Hinayana schools

concepts.name: Geographic Locations of Buddhist Councils: Mapping Significance
key_dimensions: Rajagriha (1st) → Vaishali (2nd) → Pataliputra (3rd) → Kashmir/Sri Lanka (4th): eastward to westward/southward shift
All first three councils in Magadha region — reflects Magadha's centrality to early Buddhist history
Kashmir location of Kanishka's council reflects Kushana Empire's Central Asian connections and Buddhism's silk route spread
UPSC map-based question trap: Saptaparni Cave (1st council) is near Rajagriha, not in Vaishali or Pataliputra

concepts.name: Hinayana vs. Mahayana Split: Council-wise Doctrinal Evolution
key_dimensions: Split not sudden: rooted in Second Council schism (disciplinary), evolved through Third Council's doctrinal purification, solidified by Kanishka's council
Hinayana ('lesser vehicle'): individual salvation, strict Vinaya, Arhat ideal — Theravada is surviving Hinayana school
Mahayana ('greater vehicle'): Bodhisattva ideal, universal salvation, more liberal — emerged prominently by 1st century CE
UPSC trap: 'Hinayana' is a pejorative Mahayana term; Theravada practitioners reject this label — distinguish in answer writing

concepts.name: Pali Canon vs. Sanskrit Buddhist Texts: Language and Sectarian Identity
key_dimensions: Pali Canon (Tipitaka): language of Theravada Buddhism; written down in Sri Lanka (~1st century BCE) at Vattagamani's council
Sanskrit texts: used by Sarvastivada, Mahayana schools; Mahavibhasha, Buddhacharita, Prajnaparamita sutras all in Sanskrit
Buddha himself likely spoke Magadhi Prakrit — neither Pali nor Sanskrit; UPSC trap on language of Buddha's sermons
Significance: language choice reflects geographic spread and political patronage — Pali southward, Sanskrit northward/Central Asia

concepts.name: Jain Council at Pataliputra vs. Buddhist Third Council: Avoiding Confusion
key_dimensions: Jain First Council: Pataliputra (~300 BCE) under Chandragupta Maurya, chaired by Sthulabhadra — compiled 12 Angas
Buddhist Third Council: also at Pataliputra (~250 BCE) under Ashoka — compiled Abhidhamma, dispatched missions
UPSC classic trap: both councils at Pataliputra, both during Maurya period — different religions, different purposes, different chairpersons
Jain Second Council: Vallabhi (~512 CE) — final written compilation of Jain canon; much later than any Buddhist council

concepts.name: Significance of Buddhist Councils for Textual Transmission and Sectarianism
key_dimensions: Councils served as mechanisms of canon formation, doctrinal standardization, and schism management in early Buddhism
Each council reflects a political-religious nexus: royal power used to legitimize one Buddhist faction over others
Progressive shift from oral to written transmission: First three councils = oral; Fourth = written (Pali in Sri Lanka)
Modern relevance for UPSC: understanding councils explains why Buddhism fragmented while Theravada survives intact in SE Asia

concepts.name: Ajatashatru's Role in First Council vs. His Persecution of Buddhism Debate
key_dimensions: Ajatashatru patronized First Council at Rajagriha — provided venue and material support
Paradox: Ajatashatru killed his father Bimbisara (Buddha's patron) yet later became a Buddhist supporter
His patronage ensured institutional continuity of Buddhism after Buddha's death — critical for Sangha survival
UPSC angle: distinguishing Ajatashatru (First Council patron) from Pushyamitra Shunga (Buddhist persecutor) and Ashoka (Third Council patron)

concepts.name: The Concept of Sangha Purification Across Councils
key_dimensions: Recurring theme: each council involved expelling or correcting monks who deviated from orthodox practice or doctrine
Second Council: Vajjian monks expelled for ten laxities; Third Council: 60,000 monks expelled under Ashoka-Moggaliputta Tissa
Tension between monastic purity and popular/lay Buddhism — councils repeatedly tried to maintain Vinaya discipline
UPSC analytical angle: Buddhist councils as institutional responses to the challenge of maintaining orthodoxy in a growing, decentralized religion
